Speed, support recovery and reproducible benchmarks

Source: vignettes/articles/performance.Rmd
performance.Rmd

L0glm’s shrinking active set, compiled solvers and fast GIC preset can deliver striking gains in both speed and support recovery. These examples compare complete fitting and selection workflows, with the tuning rule stated for every method. The realistic deconvolution examples are generated by the website benchmark. The README benchmark also reproduces the million-predictor LASSO comparisons.

One million predictors

The design has 500 observations, one million standard-normal predictors and 60 nonzero coefficients of either sign. L0glm uses GIC-preset ISIS plus a relaxed refit. LASSO and fully relaxed LASSO are tuned by BIC or five-fold CV.

Method Selection Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC
L0glm + ISIS GIC preset 3.49 2583 40 3 20 999937 0.777 0.787
LASSO BIC path 22.75 14789 23 612 37 999328 0.066 0.118
Relaxed LASSO BIC path 21.42 10588 21 453 39 999487 0.079 0.124
LASSO 5-fold CV 123.13 4309 17 50 43 999890 0.268 0.268
Relaxed LASSO 5-fold CV 91.76 7413 20 252 40 999688 0.120 0.156

Complete-workflow timings and false positives in the million-predictor example. L0glm uses a GIC preset; both LASSO methods use five-fold CV.

In this simulation L0glm is 35 times faster than five-fold-CV LASSO and recovers more true effects with fewer false positives. The L0glm timing includes screening and one preset fit; the other methods evaluate up to 40 native path values, with paths refitted in each CV training fold. BIC is shown alongside CV because GIC can select a null LASSO model at this dimension. All rows retain GIC as a common evaluation score. Five-fold comparisons use the same random folds.

Simulation is excluded from timings. The documented run uses one BLAS thread and eight screening threads; the design is held in memory. The L0glm time is the median of three runs. The common-scoring CV implementation used for the LASSO rows evaluates folds serially. Standalone benchmarks that call cv.glmnet() use parallel folds through cv_glmnet_parallel(). See the million-predictor tutorial for the complete data setup.

Single channel deconvolution

A realistic blurred Poisson spike train has 10,000 observations, 10,000 predictors and 1,000 true peaks. Every fit is evaluated using the original Poisson likelihood and a common GIC.

Method Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC
L0glm 0.22 102682 845 154 155 8846 0.845 0.828
LASSO 0.40 145904 950 2096 50 6904 0.470 0.467
Relaxed LASSO 0.64 122083 905 999 95 8001 0.623 0.607

L0glm uses one GIC preset with a relaxed refit. LASSO and relaxed LASSO search ten explicit lambda values using a weighted-Gaussian approximation with observation weights 1/(y+0.1). ABESS is omitted from this large example. The deconvolution tutorial shows mirrored signals and true-versus-estimated coefficient plots.

Multichannel deconvolution

The GC/MS-style simulation also has 10,000 rows, 10,000 candidate peak locations and 1,000 true peaks, with all 226 informative mass channels retained. Shared chromatographic peak times correspond to active coefficient rows; within-row coefficients describe the mass spectra.

Method Seconds GIC TP FP FN TN F1 MCC Within-row F1 Within-row MCC
L0glm 34.14 5615963 944 11 56 8989 0.966 0.962 0.909 0.864
Group LASSO 244.87 7413616 980 860 20 8140 0.690 0.685 0.842 0.768
Relaxed group LASSO 906.34 6138687 909 309 91 8691 0.820 0.802 0.853 0.782

Row F1 and MCC measure peak recovery. Within-row F1 and MCC assess spectral sparsity among correctly recovered true-positive peaks. L0glm uses the full Poisson likelihood with channel-specific working weights. Grouped glmnet uses shared row weights 1/(rowMeans(y)+0.1) for its labelled Gaussian approximation. It searches ten lambda values, with each candidate evaluated using the original Poisson likelihood. Timings include fitting, tuning and candidate scoring; L0glm uses eight outcome-fitting threads.

The deconvolution tutorial stacks observed data, ground truth and fitted coefficient heatmaps, and shows all-channel coefficient comparisons in a single column.

Native validation and OpenMP

Native validation scoring preserves multichannel OpenMP and returns the same checkpoint models as the R-validation path. This reproducible test uses 1,000 predictors, 16 channels, 60 active rows and an independent Poisson replicate for validation. Median times are from five fits, with one BLAS thread.

Backend Outcome threads Seconds Validation deviance GIC F1 MCC
General R 1 1.12 0.357612 42728.05 0.944882 0.942790
Native 1 0.08 0.357612 42728.05 0.944882 0.942790
Native 2 0.06 0.357612 42728.05 0.944882 0.942790
Native 4 0.04 0.357612 42728.05 0.944882 0.942790
Native 8 0.04 0.357612 42728.05 0.944882 0.942790

Run benchmark_native_validation.R to reproduce this comparison. Results agree across thread counts; validation predictors are shared across workers. Paired 10,000-predictor tests also preserve the unvalidated fit, with 16-channel timing 0.874 s versus 0.878 s.

Reproduce and extend

  • README benchmark source: data generation, comparisons and plots.
  • Solver/problem-size benchmark: solvers, families, matrix storage and sizes.
  • Single/multichannel benchmark: detailed signal examples and alternative methods.
  • sparseglm(): use the same comparison framework on your own data.

Timings measure complete workflows on a Windows workstation with OpenBLAS and will vary with hardware and tuning choices. F1 and MCC evaluate the known simulated support; it is never used to select models. Likelihood floors and approximation labels are explicit in the benchmark source.
